latin.535: §. X. Meliorum Seculorum finem attigimus, deterioremque initium, SEXTUM puta, quô res Veritasque Christiana in pejus ruere cœpit; Quare non præter rem Gerhard. Theodorus Mejerus, Sectionem suam sextam, Christianæ Religionis Seculi sexti Historiam exhibentem, p. 164. ita inchoat §. I.
latin.536: Et hactenus Statum Religionis Christianæ Seculo quidem V. bonum, meliorem Seculo quarto, optimum tribus primis seculis, cognovimus, nunc demum subsequuntur secula, quibus in deterius ruere incipit Christianismus, atque novam prorsus induit faciem. Deterior hic Religionis Christianæ Status, qui Seculo VI. capit, primis temporibus fuit malus, mediis pejor, ultimis vero, ante reformationem, pessimus. Atque sic à primordiis Ecclesiæ Christi usque ad Reformationem, sex distincta intervalla, seu ætates religionis christianæ, in historia annotamus. Primis quinque seculis sensim & nonnunquam sine sensu gliscere, seculo denique sexto, cursu quodam velociore atque palam ruere in Christianâ religione novos errores ac superstitiones observamus. Etiamsi verò, observante Mejero, Seculo sextô, velociori quôdam cursu novi errores ac superstitiones irruere ingruereque cœperint,
latin.537: fuerunt tamen etiam hộc Seculô nonnulli, qui & veritati Eucharisticæ constantiores adhesêre. Hos inter GELASIUS & nominis hujus & dignitatis Papalis propemodum primus numerandus, in cujus scripto quodam, Eutychi & Nestorio opposito, à Gratiano verò allegato, de Consecrat. Distinct. 2. cap. 12. hæc inter alia legimus, pro veritate, & contra Transsubstantiationem, facientia:
latin.538: Certè Sacramenta, ait, quæ sumimus, corporis & sanguinis Christi, DIVINA RES est, propter quod & per eadem, divinæ naturæ consortes efficimur: Non tamen esse desinit substantia & natura Panis & Vini; Certè IMAGO ET SIMILITUDO CORPORIS ET SANGUINIS Christi in actione Mysteriorum celebrantur.
latin.539: Gelasio suffragatur ejusdem Seculi Episcopus Hermianensis FOECUNDUS, Justiniani Imperatoris tempore florens, (Vid. Petavii Rationarium tempor. part. 1. Lib. 7. cap. 7. & 8.) Hic Librô nonô Operis sui, improprietatem verborum Christi æquè ac Spiritualem ejus in S. Eucharistia præsentiam, hisce significatum it: SACRAMENTUM inquit, corporis & sanguinis Christi, quod est in pane & poculo consecrato, corpus ejus & sanguinem dicimus: Non quod PROPRIE corpus ejus sit panis, & poculum sanguis, sed quod in se MYSTERIUM corporis sanguinisque continent, secutus scil. Doctrinam, de corporis Christi naturali localique absentiâ in terris, VIGILII Episcopi Tridentini, triginta propemodum annis illo senioris,
latin.540: cujus contra Eutychen & Nestorium disputantis verba notatu dignissima, omnem hac de re sententiam Reformatorum exponunt: Dei filius, ait ille, secundum humanitatem recessit à nobis, secundum divinitatem ait nobis: Ecce ego vobiscum sum. Per formam servi, quam abstulit à nobis in cælum, ABSENS EST NOBIS; per formam Dei, qua non recedit à nobis, in terris præsens est nobis, Lib. 1. Itemque Lib. 4. Caro Christi, quando in terra fuit, non erat utique in cælo, & nunc quia in cælo est, NON EST UTIQUE IN TERRA. Apparet unum eundemque Christum, UTRIUSQUE ESSE NATURÆ, & esse quidem ubique, secundum NATURAM divinitatis suæ, & loco contineri, secundum NATURAM humanitatis suæ.

pass_a.535: §. X. We have reached the end of the better Ages, and the beginning of the worse — the SIXTH, I mean — in which the Christian matter and Truth began to rush into the worse; Wherefore it is not beside the point that Gerhard. Theodorus Mejerus, exhibiting his sixth Section, the History of the Christian Religion of the sixth Age, p. 164, begins thus §. I.
pass_a.536: And thus far we have known the State of the Christian Religion in the Vth Age indeed good, better in the fourth Age, best in the three first ages; now at last follow the ages in which Christianity begins to rush into the worse, and puts on an altogether new face. This worse State of the Christian Religion, which takes its start in the VIth Age, was in the first times bad, in the middle worse, but in the last, before the reformation, worst. And so from the beginnings of Christ’s Church all the way to the Reformation, we mark in history six distinct intervals, or ages of the Christian religion. In the first five ages we observe new errors and superstitions in the Christian religion swelling gradually and sometimes without sense; finally in the sixth age, by a swifter course and openly, rushing. Although indeed, Mejerus observing, in the sixth Age new errors and superstitions began to rush in and press in by a certain swifter course,
pass_a.537: yet there were even in this Age some who adhered more constantly also to the Eucharistic truth. Among these GELASIUS is to be numbered almost the first both of this name and of Papal dignity, in a certain writing of whose, opposed to Eutyches and Nestorius, but alleged by Gratian, de Consecrat. Distinct. 2. cap. 12., we read among other things these sayings that make for the truth and against Transubstantiation:
pass_a.538: Certainly the Sacraments, he says, which we take, of the body and blood of Christ, are a DIVINE THING, on account of which and through the same we are made partakers of the divine nature: Yet the substance and nature of Bread and Wine does not cease to be; Certainly the IMAGE AND LIKENESS OF THE BODY AND BLOOD of Christ are celebrated in the action of the Mysteries.
pass_a.539: To Gelasius there votes the Bishop of Hermiane of the same Age, FOECUNDUS, flourishing in the time of the Emperor Justinian (see Petavius’s Rationarium of times, part 1, Book 7, ch. 7 and 8). He in the ninth Book of his Work signifies by these things the impropriety of Christ’s words equally and His Spiritual presence in the Sacred Eucharist: The SACRAMENT, he says, of the body and blood of Christ, which is in the consecrated bread and cup, we call His body and blood: Not that the bread is PROPERLY His body, and the cup blood, but that they contain in themselves the MYSTERY of body and blood — following namely the Doctrine, concerning the natural and local absence of Christ’s body on earth, of VIGILIUS Bishop of Trent, older than him by nearly thirty years,
pass_a.540: whose words disputing against Eutyches and Nestorius, most worthy of note, set out the whole sentence of the Reformers on this matter: The Son of God, he says, according to humanity withdrew from us; according to divinity He is with us: Behold I am with you. By the form of a servant, which He took away from us into heaven, HE IS ABSENT FROM US; by the form of God, by which He does not withdraw from us, He is present to us on earth (Book 1). Likewise Book 4: The flesh of Christ, when it was on earth, was certainly not in heaven, and now because it is in heaven, IT IS CERTAINLY NOT ON EARTH. It appears that one and the same Christ IS OF BOTH NATURES, and is indeed everywhere according to the NATURE of His divinity, and is contained in a place according to the NATURE of His humanity.

535: §.X: we have reached the end of the better ages and the start of the worse — the SIXTH — when Christian truth began to rush downhill.
Mejerus opens his sixth section (Christian Religion of the sixth age, p. 164) with that framing.
536: Mejerus: Age V still good; IV better; the first three best — then ages follow in which Christianity puts on a new, worse face.
Six ages from the Church’s beginnings to the Reformation: errors creep in the first five; in the sixth they rush in faster and openly.
537: Yet even in this age some clung more constantly to Eucharistic truth.
Among them GELASIUS — almost first of the papal name and dignity — in a writing against Eutyches and Nestorius (Gratian, de Consecrat. Dist. 2 c. 12), for truth and against Transubstantiation.
538: Gelasius: the Sacraments of Christ’s body and blood that we take are a DIVINE THING — through them we share the divine nature.
Yet bread and wine do not cease to be in substance and nature; in the Mysteries’ action the IMAGE AND LIKENESS of body and blood are celebrated.
539: Foecundus of Hermiane (same age; Justinian’s time) seconds Gelasius: Christ’s words are improper speech; presence in the Eucharist is spiritual.

We call the sacrament in consecrated bread and cup His body and blood — not that bread is PROPERLY body or cup blood, but that they contain the MYSTERY — following Vigilius of Trent on the body’s natural local absence on earth.
540: Vigilius (against Eutyches and Nestorius) states the Reformers’ sentence: according to humanity the Son withdrew; according to divinity He is with us.

By the servant-form taken into heaven He is ABSENT; by the form of God He is present on earth. Flesh once on earth was not in heaven; now in heaven it is NOT ON EARTH. One Christ of BOTH NATURES — everywhere by divinity, place-bound by humanity.
